what_it_does: A modern graphics processing unit (GPU) has a fixed, balanced mix of compute units (called Streaming Multiprocessors, or SMs — the engines that run calculations) and memory capacity. When two different programs share a GPU, one might need mostly computation while the other is mostly waiting on memory, so the fixed balance wastes resources. UGPU is a system that carves a single physical GPU into uneven slices on the fly, giving each program exactly as much compute or memory as its workload needs. The hard part is moving data between memory regions when the balance shifts; UGPU solves this with a technique called PageMove, which uses the fact that all memory chips in a stacked memory package (called High-Bandwidth Memory, or HBM — a fast, vertically stacked memory chip mounted right next to the GPU) share physical vertical wiring called Through-Silicon Vias (TSVs), enabling many pages of data to move in parallel rather than one at a time.
